## Overview  
When traders look for a platform that blends powerful charting, reliable data, and user‑friendly tools, two names often rise to the top: [TradingView](https://in.tradingview.com/?aff_id=167054) and Thinkorswim. Both cater to active investors, but they serve slightly different audiences. TradingView shines as a web‑first, socially driven charting suite that works across brokers, while Thinkorswim (often called TOS) is the flagship desktop platform of TD Ameritrade, offering deep integration with a full‑service brokerage. This comparison breaks down the core differences so you can decide which environment fits your style.

## Charting Tools  
TradingView’s charting engine is built for speed and flexibility. You can open multiple charts in a single layout, drag‑and‑drop studies, and switch timeframes with a single click. The platform supports over 100 chart types, including Renko, Kagi, and Point‑and‑Figure, and lets you create custom Pine Script indicators.  

Thinkorswim offers equally robust charts, but the interface feels more traditional. Studies are organized in a dropdown menu, and you can layer unlimited studies on a single pane. TOS excels in advanced drawing tools like Fibonacci extensions, Gann fans, and market profile, which are buried deeper in TradingView’s menu. If you prefer a desktop‑centric experience with extensive built‑in studies, Thinkorswim may feel more complete out of the box.

## Indicators and Studies  
Both platforms provide a library of technical indicators, yet the way you access them differs. TradingView’s public script library lets you browse thousands of community‑created Pine Scripts, copy them with one click, and even modify the code directly in the browser. This openness encourages experimentation and rapid sharing.  

Thinkorswim’s thinkScript language is powerful but less accessible to newcomers. You need to write or import scripts within the desktop client, and sharing requires uploading to the thinkScript Community or emailing the file. While thinkScript can handle complex backtesting and automated alerts, the learning curve is steeper than Pine Script.

## Order Execution  
Thinkorswim shines when it comes to executing trades. Because it’s tied to TD Ameritrade, you can place market, limit, stop, and conditional orders directly from the chart with a single click. The platform also supports advanced order types like OCO, bracket, and multi‑leg options spreads.  

TradingView, by contrast, is primarily a charting and analysis tool. It offers broker integration through partners such as Tradestation, Forex.com, and Interactive Brokers, but the execution experience varies by broker and may require leaving the chart to confirm orders. If seamless, all‑in‑one trading is a priority, Thinkorswim has the edge.

## Pricing and Plans  
TradingView follows a freemium model. The free tier gives you limited indicators per chart and one saved layout. Pro ($14.95/month) adds more indicators, multiple chart layouts, and priority support. Pro+ ($29.95/month) and Premium ($59.95/month) unlock even more features like server‑side alerts and unlimited charts.  

Thinkorswim is free to use if you have a funded TD Ameritrade account. There are no subscription fees for the platform itself; you only pay standard trading commissions and fees (which are $0 for stocks/ETFs and $0.65 per options contract). If you already trade with TD Ameritrade, Thinkorswim comes at no extra cost, making it attractive for budget‑conscious traders.

## Community Features  
One of TradingView’s biggest draws is its social network. Users can publish ideas, follow other traders, comment on charts, and host live streams. The platform’s built‑in chat and screener community foster collaboration and idea generation.  

Thinkorswim offers a more subdued community experience. The thinkScript Community lets you share scripts, but there’s no public feed of trade ideas or chart commentary. Interaction happens mainly through TD Ameritrade’s client forums or third‑party discords. If you thrive on sharing and discovering strategies in real time, TradingView’s social layer is stronger.

## Mobile Experience  
TradingView’s mobile apps (iOS/Android) mirror the desktop experience closely. You can view charts, apply indicators, set alerts, and even publish ideas from your phone. The interface feels lightweight and responsive, making it ideal for traders who need to check setups on the go.  

Thinkorswim Mobile provides solid functionality for watching quotes, placing trades, and viewing basic charts, but advanced studies and custom thinkScript aren’t as fluid on a small screen. The app works best for order management rather than deep analysis. For pure charting on a smartphone, TradingView generally wins.

## Pros and Cons  

**TradingView**  
- Pros: Web‑based, no install needed; extensive Pine Script library; strong social community; excellent multi‑chart layout; flexible pricing tiers.  
- Cons: Order execution depends on broker integration; advanced backtesting less intuitive; free tier limited.

**Thinkorswim**  
- Pros: Deep broker integration with TD Ameritrade; powerful thinkScript for complex strategies; free with account; robust desktop drawing tools; reliable order types.  
- Cons: Desktop‑only (web version limited); steeper learning curve
